newsitem.title: USA: GFOA tells NASD it backs bond fund risk ratings.
newsitem.headline: GFOA tells NASD it backs bond fund risk ratings.

text.p: Government finance officers told the National Association of Securities Dealers that they back the inclusion of risk ratings developed by ratings agencies in sales literature for bond mutual funds.

In a five-page comment letter delivered late Monday to NASD, the Government Finance Officers Association said that since credit ratings have been used successfully in brochures and other sales literature for bond financings, there is no reason why risk ratings also would not be useful.

Standard & Poor's Ratings Group in 1994 launched a service to rate the risk of bond funds, including municipal funds. But NASD, which regulates mutual fund advertising, ruled that funds may not use such ratings in sales literature.
NASD worried that the ratings could mislead investors because they hinge on "assumptions and speculation" about the economy in general and about a company's solvency.
Nevertheless, NASD reopened the issue in December by calling for a new round of comments, due on February 24, 1997.
In 1995, GFOA issued a "recommended practice" that finance officers invest in "only those funds that seek market risk ratings from rating agencies."
Opponents of the ratings say that rating agencies should not be in the business of "predicting" a municipality's performance.
But GFOA said on Monday that rating agencies could put a disclaimer on risk ratings saying they are, in fact, predictions.
GFOA aragued that credit ratings, which are used broadly in the muni market, themselves have a predictive flavor.

Critics of bond fund risk ratings also warn that permitting them in sales literature could backfire for the market. Municipalities that get undesirable ratings could simply bury the information, they say.
But GFOA said that is not possible since once a fund is rated the information usually circulates anyway.
The next step for NASD, if it decides to proceed on the fund risk rating issue, would be to propose a formal rule for public comment.
